issues.legal_issue: An objection that an eviction petition is not maintainable because partners of a named partnership firm were not joined cannot be raised for the first time at the special-leave stage when the defect could have been cured earlier.
material_facts: The eviction petition named the tenant firm and another firm alleged to be the sub-tenant, but did not join the other firm’s partners individually.
The objection to the parties’ joinder was not raised in the trial court, the first appellate court, or the High Court; it was raised for the first time at the special-leave stage.
The landlord could have amended the petition to join the partners if the objection had been raised earlier.
issues.conclusion: The objection was rejected because it was raised at a very late stage and could have been addressed by amendment earlier in the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, a party cannot raise at the special-leave stage an objection to the maintainability of an eviction petition that was not raised earlier and could have been cured by amendment. Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm and others v. Shikharchand, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 268, was distinguishable: the objection there had been raised at the earliest stage, and the Court treated the defect as a correctable misdescription.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.objection_first_raised_at_special_leave: The party first raises the objection to the other party’s joinder at the special-leave stage.
predicates.joinder_defect_could_be_cured_earlier: The party seeking relief could have corrected the joinder defect by amendment if the objection had been raised earlier.

issues.definition: When an appeal is brought by special leave and a curable joinder objection is first raised at that stage, the objection is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A finding of unlawful subletting may be supported by evidence that another business occupied the premises and by an inference from the tenant’s failure to produce relevant accounts after notice.
material_facts: The eviction proceeding alleged unlawful subletting without the landlord’s consent under Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960.
Evidence showed that the alleged sub-tenant carried on business at the premises, including during a period when the tenant firm had ceased doing business there.
After receiving notice to produce income-tax returns, assessment orders, account books, and ledgers for the relevant period, the tenant firm and the other firm did not produce them.
The trial court inferred that the accounts, if produced, would have shown that the tenant received rent from the other firm.
issues.conclusion: The evidence and the non-production of the requested records supported the finding of unlawful subletting, so the challenge to that finding failed.
issues.legal_principle: For an eviction ground under Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960, unlawful subletting may be inferred from the circumstances, including a third party carrying on business in the premises and the failure to produce relevant records after notice where those records could have shown receipt of rent.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and third_party_business_on_premises and tenant_absent_during_some_occupation and relevant_records_withheld_after_notice

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction on a ground governed by rent-control law.
predicates.third_party_business_on_premises: A business other than the tenant’s carries on business in the rented premises.
predicates.tenant_absent_during_some_occupation: The other business occupies or operates in the premises during a period when the tenant is not carrying on business there.
predicates.relevant_records_withheld_after_notice: The tenant or other business fails to produce relevant financial or business records after being asked to do so by notice.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, third-party business at the premises, tenant absence during some of that occupation, and withholding relevant records after notice permit unlawful subletting to be inferred.

issues.legal_issue: A request for detailed reappraisal of evidence does not require the Supreme Court to undertake that exercise in an appeal under Article 136.
material_facts: The appellants asked the Supreme Court to undertake a detailed scrutiny and reappraisal of the evidence.
The matter was before the Supreme Court in an appeal by special leave under Article 136.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to undertake the requested detailed reappraisal of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it was not called upon to undertake detailed scrutiny and reappraisal of the evidence in an appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.article_136_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal under the Supreme Court’s special-leave jurisdiction.
predicates.detailed_evidence_reappraisal_requested: A party asks the Court to conduct detailed scrutiny and reappraisal of the evidence.

issues.definition: When a party requests detailed evidence reappraisal in an appeal under special-leave jurisdiction, the Court is not required to undertake it.
